questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a resting tremor of the left hand, slowness and stiffness. A dopamine-transporter scan shows reduced uptake, most marked in the right putamen. Loss of which neurons best explains this?
o: Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta
Neurons of the internal globus pallidus
Medium spiny neurons of the caudate nucleus
Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area
e: Correct. They project to the putamen and caudate (nigrostriatal pathway); their loss causes the motor signs of Parkinson's disease.
The subthalamic nucleus becomes overactive in Parkinson's disease; it is a stimulation target, not the site of neuron loss.
GPi is the output of the basal ganglia; its activity changes, but it is not where dopamine neurons are lost.
These are lost in Huntington's disease, which causes chorea rather than parkinsonism.
These supply the ventral striatum and cortex; they are relatively spared early in Parkinson's disease.
questions.obj: Parkinson's motor signs come from loss of nigral dopamine neurons, with dopamine loss first and greatest in the putamen; signs appear on the opposite side of the body.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a 72-year-old woman speaks fluently but her sentences make little sense. She does not follow spoken commands and cannot repeat a phrase. Where is the lesion most likely?
o: Left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis)
e: Correct. Damage to this classical Wernicke region causes fluent speech with poor comprehension and repetition.
This is Broca's area; damage causes non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
Damage causes weakness of the opposite face and arm and slurred speech, not loss of comprehension.
In most right-handed people language is left-dominant; right-sided damage mainly affects speech melody (prosody).
This causes a visual field defect, not aphasia.
questions.obj: Fluent aphasia with poor comprehension points to the left posterior superior temporal cortex; non-fluent aphasia points to the left inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man speaks in short, effortful phrases and is frustrated by it. He understands questions well. Which structure is most likely damaged?
o: Left inferior frontal gyrus, opercular and triangular parts
e: Correct. This is Broca's area: speech production and grammar.
Damage here causes problems with reading, writing and arithmetic (Gerstmann-type signs).
Damage to the posterior temporal language region impairs comprehension rather than fluency.
Causes unsteady gait and slurred (ataxic) speech, but language itself is intact.
Affects memory for words and events, not speech fluency.
questions.obj: Non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia localises to the left inferior frontal gyrus.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman suddenly cannot move her right leg; her face and arm are normal. Which part of the motor cortex is affected?
o: Medial (paracentral) part of the left precentral gyrus
Lateral part of the left precentral gyrus
Medial part of the right precentral gyrus
e: Correct. The leg is represented on the medial surface, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery.
This area controls the face and hand (middle cerebral artery territory).
This would weaken the left leg: motor control is crossed.
This is sensory cortex; damage causes numbness, not paralysis.
Damage causes problems starting movements, not isolated paralysis of one leg.
questions.obj: The motor homunculus places the leg medially and the face and hand laterally; the cortex controls the opposite side.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man develops sudden wild, flinging movements of his left arm and leg. Which structure is most likely affected by a small stroke?
e: Correct. Damage causes contralateral hemiballismus.
This would affect the right side of the body.
Caudate damage causes changes in behaviour and motivation more than violent flinging movements.
This would cause clumsiness of the right side (ipsilateral).
Usually causes sensory loss on the right side.
questions.obj: Hemiballismus localises to the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

questions.stem: After herpes simplex encephalitis, a 40-year-old woman cannot form new memories of events, while old memories and intelligence are largely preserved. Which structures are most likely damaged on both sides?
e: Correct. Bilateral hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia.
Bilateral amygdala damage changes fear and emotional responses but does not abolish new memory.
Affects working memory and planning, not new long-term memory.
Causes blindness, not amnesia.
Affects motor learning, not memory for events.
questions.obj: The hippocampus is essential for forming new memories of events (declarative memory).

questions.stem: A man with a right parietal stroke ignores the left side of his plate and shaves only the right side of his face. Where is the lesion most likely?
e: Correct. Right parietal damage causes left-sided neglect.
Left parietal damage rarely causes marked neglect; it more often affects language and praxis.
This causes a visual field loss, which patients usually notice; neglect is a failure of attention.
Causes weakness, not neglect.
Causes disconnection syndromes, not unilateral neglect.
questions.obj: Spatial attention is right-hemisphere dominant: right parietal damage causes neglect of the left side.

questions.stem: A patient lies awake but does not speak or move spontaneously, although he can follow his eyes to people. MRI shows bilateral damage to the medial frontal lobes. Which structure is most important for this 'akinetic mutism'?
e: Correct. Bilateral anterior cingulate damage removes the drive to act.
Linked to self-referential thought and memory, not the will to act.
Would cause paralysis, not lack of initiative with preserved strength.
Affects vision.
Affects coordination.
questions.obj: The anterior cingulate cortex links motivation to action; bilateral damage can cause akinetic mutism.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a tremor that worsens as her finger approaches her nose, and she overshoots targets with her right hand. Where is the lesion?
e: Correct. Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral intention tremor and dysmetria.
Cerebellar signs are on the same side as the lesion.
Causes a resting tremor on the right, which improves with movement.
Mainly causes unsteady gait and trunk instability.
Causes weakness, not intention tremor.
questions.obj: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia; the vermis controls the trunk and gait.

questions.stem: Which structure is the main source of acetylcholine for the cerebral cortex, and loses neurons early in Alzheimer's disease?
e: Correct. Its loss is the reason cholinesterase inhibitors are used.
Main source of noradrenaline.
Main source of serotonin.
Main source of striatal dopamine.
Produces hormones and controls body functions; not the cortical acetylcholine source.
questions.obj: The cholinergic hypothesis of Alzheimer's disease rests on loss of basal forebrain neurons.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has bilateral damage to the temporal poles and amygdalae after an infection. He becomes unusually calm, puts objects in his mouth and shows reduced fear. Which syndrome is this?
e: Correct. Bilateral amygdala and anterior temporal damage causes placidity, hyperorality and altered sexual behaviour.
Caused by thiamine deficiency affecting the mammillary bodies and thalamus; leads to amnesia and confabulation.
Left angular gyrus: problems with writing, calculation, finger naming and left-right orientation.
Bilateral parieto-occipital damage: problems with visual attention and reaching.
A language disorder from posterior superior temporal damage.
questions.obj: The amygdala is central to fear and emotional evaluation; bilateral damage causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome.

questions.stem: Which structure relays almost all sensory information, except smell, to the cerebral cortex?
e: Correct. Specific thalamic nuclei relay vision, hearing, touch and taste.
Controls hormones and body functions; not the main sensory relay.
Evaluates emotional significance.
Part of the basal ganglia motor loop.
Coordinates movement.
questions.obj: The thalamus is the gateway to the cortex for every sense except smell.

questions.stem: Where is the primary auditory cortex?
e: Correct. It lies on the upper surface of the temporal lobe.
Involved in reading and meaning.
This is primary visual cortex.
This is primary somatosensory cortex.
Processes body signals, taste and emotion.
questions.obj: Heschl's gyrus is the first cortical station for sound.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old has a stroke in the right occipital lobe. What is the most likely visual finding?
o: Left homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing
Blindness in the right eye only
Inability to recognise faces with normal visual fields
e: Correct. The right visual cortex receives the left visual field of both eyes.
That would follow a left occipital lesion.
Caused by compression of the optic chiasm, e.g. by a pituitary tumour.
Caused by damage to the right eye or optic nerve before the chiasm.
That is prosopagnosia, from fusiform gyrus damage.
questions.obj: Post-chiasmal lesions cause homonymous field defects on the opposite side.

questions.stem: A woman can see faces clearly but cannot recognise her own family by their faces; she recognises them by voice. Which region is most likely damaged?
o: Fusiform gyrus (usually right or both sides)
e: Correct. This causes prosopagnosia.
Would cause loss of vision, not selective face recognition loss.
Involved in hearing and speech.
Involved in body awareness and phonology.
Would affect memory in general, including for voices.
questions.obj: The fusiform face area on the underside of the temporal lobe is specialised for faces.

questions.stem: Which is the most studied deep brain stimulation target for advanced Parkinson's disease with motor fluctuations?
e: Correct. STN stimulation is the best-studied option; the internal globus pallidus is the alternative.
Studied for psychiatric conditions, not Parkinson's motor fluctuations.
Not a movement target.
An experimental target for depression.
Not a movement target.
questions.obj: STN and GPi are the two established DBS targets for Parkinson's disease; STN is the best studied.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old has lost his sense of the heartbeat and of disgust after a stroke, and reports feeling 'disconnected from his body'. Which region is most likely involved?
e: Correct. It integrates body signals (interoception) into feelings.
Visual processing.
Balance and posture.
Goal-directed learning.
Object shape recognition.
questions.obj: The anterior insula turns signals from inside the body into conscious feelings.

questions.stem: A railway worker survives an iron rod passing through his frontal lobes; afterwards he is impulsive and socially inappropriate, but his memory and intelligence seem intact. Which region was most likely damaged?
e: Correct. Damage changes social behaviour, judgement and decision-making.
Would cause weakness.
Would cause memory loss.
Would affect vision.
Would affect coordination.
questions.obj: The orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex link emotion and values to behaviour.

questions.stem: Which pair of regions forms the core of the default mode network?
o: Medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex/precuneus
Primary motor and primary sensory cortex
Anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate
Dorsolateral prefrontal and posterior parietal cortex
e: Correct. These cortical midline hubs are active during self-related thought and rest.
These form the sensorimotor network.
These form the core of the salience network.
These form the central executive network.
Sensory areas, not the default mode network.
questions.obj: The default mode network is anchored in the medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate/precuneus cortex.

questions.stem: Which structure contains the body's master clock (suprachiasmatic nucleus) and controls hunger, temperature and hormone release?
e: Correct. In this atlas it is part of the 'hypothalamus and ventral diencephalon' structure.
The sensory relay above it.
Makes melatonin under the control of the suprachiasmatic nucleus, but is not the clock itself.
Fear and emotion.
Breathing and sleep regulation, but not the master clock.
questions.obj: The hypothalamus controls body homeostasis and contains the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

questions.stem: Why is levodopa almost always combined with carbidopa or benserazide?
o: They block the conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the brain
They help levodopa cross the blood-brain barrier
They block MAO-B in the brain
They slow loss of dopamine neurons
e: Correct. More levodopa reaches the brain and nausea from dopamine in the blood is reduced; they do not cross the blood-brain barrier.
Levodopa crosses via an amino-acid transporter; carbidopa does not help it cross.
That is what dopamine agonists do.
That is the action of selegiline, rasagiline and safinamide.
No treatment has been shown to slow Parkinson's disease.
questions.obj: Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors increase the brain availability of levodopa and reduce peripheral side effects.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old with newly diagnosed Parkinson's disease has symptoms that affect his work. According to the AAN 2021 guideline, which initial treatment gives the greatest motor benefit?
e: Correct. It gives more motor benefit than dopamine agonists, at the cost of more dyskinesia over time.
An alternative in selected people, with less motor benefit and more impulse-control problems.
Mainly used later, for dyskinesia.
Not offered in early disease without motor fluctuations.
Sometimes used for tremor in young people, but not the most effective initial therapy.
questions.obj: Levodopa is the most effective initial treatment for the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: Six months after starting pramipexole, a 58-year-old man begins gambling compulsively. What is the most likely cause?
o: An impulse-control disorder caused by the dopamine agonist
Disease progression in the substantia nigra
A manic episode of bipolar disorder
e: Correct. This risk is higher with dopamine agonists than with levodopa.
Not typical of compulsive gambling at this stage.
Progression worsens movement; it does not cause compulsive gambling.
Causes agitation, fever, tremor and muscle twitching, not gambling.
Possible in theory, but a drug side effect is far more likely here.
questions.obj: Dopamine agonists carry a higher risk of impulse-control disorders than levodopa; patients should be warned and monitored.

questions.stem: A woman with Parkinson's disease for 6 years notices that each levodopa dose wears off after about 3 hours. Which addition is supported for treating such motor fluctuations?
o: A COMT inhibitor such as entacapone or opicapone
e: Correct. It slows levodopa breakdown so each dose lasts longer; MAO-B inhibitors and dopamine agonists are other options.
This would worsen symptoms and can be dangerous.
Would worsen parkinsonism (most block D2 receptors).
Not a treatment for wearing-off.
No benefit for motor fluctuations.
questions.obj: Wearing-off is treated by prolonging levodopa action (COMT or MAO-B inhibitors), adding an agonist, or changing the levodopa formulation.

questions.stem: A man with Parkinson's disease has troublesome involuntary writhing movements at the peak of each levodopa dose. Which drug is used specifically for this?
e: Correct. It reduces levodopa-induced dyskinesia; it is thought to act by blocking NMDA receptors.
Would worsen peak-dose dyskinesia.
Has no effect on its own.
Prolongs dopamine and may worsen dyskinesia.
Would improve dyskinesia only by worsening parkinsonism; avoided.
questions.obj: Amantadine is the oral drug with evidence for levodopa-induced dyskinesia.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with Parkinson's disease for 5 years has early motor fluctuations despite optimised tablets. Which statement about deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus is best supported?
o: It can be offered once fluctuations are present, including early fluctuations
It is only for end-stage disease
It should be offered at diagnosis
It stops the disease from progressing
It works best in people who never responded to levodopa
e: Correct. EARLYSTIM showed benefit over medical therapy in people with early motor complications.
Trial evidence supports earlier use once fluctuations appear.
Not offered without fluctuations.
It improves symptoms and quality of life but does not slow the disease.
Good response to levodopa predicts good response to DBS.
questions.obj: STN-DBS is indicated for motor fluctuations not controlled by medication, including in earlier disease.

questions.stem: In typical Alzheimer's disease, where do tau tangles appear first in the cortex?
e: Correct. Tau pathology begins in the entorhinal cortex and spreads to the hippocampus and wider cortex.
Affected late in typical disease.
Spared until late.
Largely spared.
Not an early site of tau in Alzheimer's disease.
questions.obj: Alzheimer tau pathology starts in the medial temporal lobe, explaining early memory loss.

questions.stem: How does donepezil work?
o: It inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine in the synapse
e: Correct.
That is memantine.
That is what anti-amyloid antibodies do.
That is levodopa in Parkinson's disease.
That is an SSRI.
questions.obj: Cholinesterase inhibitors compensate for the loss of cholinergic neurons; they give small symptomatic benefit.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's dementia is already taking donepezil. Which drug has high-certainty evidence of a small additional benefit?
e: Correct. A moderate-affinity NMDA receptor blocker with a small benefit in moderate to severe disease.
Only studied in early disease (MCI or mild dementia).
A Parkinson's drug.
Not a dementia treatment.
Increases risks in dementia and does not improve cognition.
questions.obj: Memantine is used in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease, alone or with a cholinesterase inhibitor.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with mild Alzheimer's dementia and confirmed brain amyloid lives in the EU and takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Which statement about lecanemab is correct?
o: Under EU conditions he would not be treated, because of ongoing anticoagulation
He can start immediately without MRI monitoring
Lecanemab is given only in severe dementia
e: Correct. The EMA restricted lecanemab in people on anticoagulants (and in APOE4 homozygotes) because of bleeding risk.
MRI monitoring for ARIA is required.
It modestly slows decline in early disease; it does not reverse it.
It is studied and used only in early disease.
It is an antibody against amyloid-beta protofibrils.
questions.obj: Anti-amyloid antibodies carry a risk of brain swelling and bleeding (ARIA); anticoagulation increases bleeding risk and excludes treatment in the EU.

questions.stem: In the Clarity AD trial, what was the effect of lecanemab after 18 months in early Alzheimer's disease?
o: It slowed decline on the CDR-SB scale by 0.45 points compared with placebo
It had no effect on amyloid PET
It worked only in severe dementia
e: Correct. A modest slowing of decline, with clear lowering of amyloid on PET.
Decline continued, more slowly.
Scores still worsened in both groups.
Amyloid fell by about 59 centiloids.
The trial enrolled only early disease.
questions.obj: Anti-amyloid antibodies give modest slowing of decline in early disease; they are not cures.

questions.stem: Which test is used to confirm that cognitive impairment is due to Alzheimer's disease before considering anti-amyloid treatment?
o: Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid amyloid/tau biomarkers
A genetic test for APOE alone
e: Correct. Biomarker confirmation of amyloid is required.
Excludes other causes but cannot show amyloid.
Not used to confirm amyloid.
APOE affects risk and ARIA risk but does not diagnose the disease.
Used for parkinsonian syndromes.
questions.obj: Alzheimer's disease is now diagnosed biologically, with amyloid and tau biomarkers, in memory clinics.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man has weakness and wasting of the hands with fasciculations, together with brisk reflexes and spasticity in the legs. Sensation is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Correct. A combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs without sensory loss is typical.
Usually causes sensory symptoms and episodes that improve.
Causes sensory loss and reduced reflexes.
Causes fatigable weakness without fasciculations or spasticity.
Causes slowness and rigidity, not wasting with fasciculations.
questions.obj: ALS affects both upper motor neurons (motor cortex) and lower motor neurons (brainstem and spinal cord).

questions.stem: What is the expected benefit of riluzole in ALS?
o: It prolongs median survival by about 2 to 3 months
e: Correct, according to a Cochrane review.
No current drug stops ALS.
It does not reverse weakness.
Riluzole is used in ALS generally; tofersen is SOD1-specific.
Its benefit is modest but supported by trials.
questions.obj: Riluzole is a modest disease-modifying treatment for ALS.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old with ALS carries a pathogenic SOD1 variant. How does tofersen work?
o: It is an antisense oligonucleotide that lowers production of SOD1 protein
It is an antibody that clears SOD1 aggregates from the blood
e: Correct. It is given into the spinal fluid.
It acts on the SOD1 message (mRNA) inside cells.
That is riluzole.
That is edaravone.
It reduces, rather than replaces, SOD1.
questions.obj: Gene-targeted silencing is now possible for ALS caused by SOD1 variants.

questions.stem: What did the phase 3 ADORE trial show for daily oral edaravone in ALS?
o: It did not slow functional decline compared with placebo over 48 weeks
It halved the rate of decline
It prolonged survival by two years
It was effective only in SOD1-ALS
It caused severe liver damage in most patients
e: Correct. It was well tolerated but ineffective at the tested dose.
No significant difference was found.
Not shown.
Not shown.
Adverse events were similar to placebo.
questions.obj: A drug that seemed promising in a selected subgroup failed in a broader phase 3 trial: subgroup findings need confirmation.

questions.stem: A woman with ALS has morning headaches, poor sleep and breathlessness lying flat. Which supportive treatment is most appropriate?
e: Correct. It treats respiratory muscle weakness, a key part of multidisciplinary care.
Higher doses do not help breathing.
Could worsen breathing.
Does not treat respiratory failure.
Not relevant to ALS.
questions.obj: Breathing and nutritional support are central to ALS care.

questions.stem: PET studies in schizophrenia most consistently show which dopamine abnormality?
o: Increased presynaptic dopamine synthesis and release, mainly in the associative (dorsal) striatum
A large increase in D2 receptors in drug-naive patients
Increased dopamine mainly in the nucleus accumbens
e: Correct. The limbic (ventral) striatum showed no significant increase in a meta-analysis.
The receptor increase is small and not seen in drug-naive patients.
No alteration was found.
This 'mesolimbic' version was not supported.
Presynaptic elevation is one of the most replicated findings.
questions.obj: The main dopamine abnormality in schizophrenia is presynaptic and dorsal; current drugs act downstream at D2 receptors.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia has had no adequate response to two different antipsychotics at adequate dose and duration. What is the recommended next step?
e: Correct. It is the treatment of choice for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
Less effective than clozapine at this stage.
Not an antipsychotic.
Increases relapse risk.
Not a treatment for psychosis.
questions.obj: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (two failed antipsychotics) is treated with clozapine.

questions.stem: A patient starting clozapine asks why he needs regular blood tests. What is the main reason?
o: To detect a fall in white blood cells (neutropenia/agranulocytosis)
To detect high blood sugar only
e: Correct. This rare but serious side effect requires monitoring.
Not measured in the blood.
Not the main reason.
Metabolic monitoring is also needed, but neutropenia is the specific reason for regular counts.
Blood tests do not diagnose schizophrenia.
questions.obj: Clozapine requires blood count monitoring because of the risk of agranulocytosis (standard prescribing knowledge).

questions.stem: How does xanomeline-trospium differ from earlier antipsychotics?
o: Xanomeline stimulates muscarinic M1/M4 receptors and does not block D2 receptors; trospium limits side effects outside the brain
It is a stronger D2 blocker
e: Correct.
It has no direct D2 blockade.
That is an SSRI.
That is ulotaront.
It is a small-molecule combination.
questions.obj: Muscarinic agonism is the first approved antipsychotic mechanism without direct D2 blockade.

questions.stem: A man starting haloperidol develops stiffness, a shuffling gait and tremor. Blockade of D2 receptors in which pathway explains this?
e: Correct. D2 blockade in the dorsal striatum causes drug-induced parkinsonism.
D2 blockade here raises prolactin.
Linked to negative and cognitive symptoms.
A serotonin pathway.
A motor tract, not dopaminergic.
questions.obj: Extrapyramidal side effects come from D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal system.

questions.stem: Large exome studies (SCHEMA) found rare damaging variants in 10 genes that raise schizophrenia risk. Which of these encodes a glutamate NMDA receptor subunit?
e: Correct. It supports the involvement of glutamate signalling.
A chromatin regulator.
A ubiquitin ligase component.
A nuclear export protein.
A regulator of the cytoskeleton.
questions.obj: Rare-variant genetics links schizophrenia to synaptic and glutamate genes.

questions.stem: What happened with iclepertin, a GlyT1 inhibitor intended to improve cognition in schizophrenia?
o: It did not improve cognition in three phase 3 trials
It replaced clozapine for treatment resistance
It was effective only in first-episode psychosis
e: Correct.
It was not.
Not shown.
Not shown.
Not shown.
questions.obj: Cognitive impairment in schizophrenia remains without an effective drug treatment.

questions.stem: Which treatment for bipolar disorder has evidence of reducing suicide compared with placebo?
e: Correct.
Useful for depression and maintenance, but suicide reduction is not established in the same way.
An antidepressant; not a mood stabiliser.
Treats mania but has no specific suicide evidence.
Not a bipolar maintenance treatment.
questions.obj: Lithium is the mood stabiliser with the strongest evidence against suicide.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar disorder who may want children asks about valproate. What is the key safety point in Europe?
o: It causes birth defects and developmental problems; it must not be used in anyone who could become pregnant unless strict pregnancy-prevention conditions are met
It is the safest mood stabiliser in pregnancy
It only matters during the last month of pregnancy
It is banned for all women
e: Correct.
It carries the highest risk among common options.
The risk includes early pregnancy, often before pregnancy is known.
It is restricted, not banned.
Folic acid does not remove valproate's risks.
questions.obj: Valproate is highly teratogenic and restricted in people of childbearing potential.

questions.stem: Which treatment is NOT listed as first-line for acute mania in the CANMAT/ISBD 2018 guidelines?
e: Correct. Antidepressant monotherapy can worsen mania and is not recommended.
First-line.
First-line.
First-line.
First-line.
questions.obj: Acute mania is treated with mood stabilisers or antipsychotics, not antidepressants.

questions.stem: A man on lithium starts ibuprofen and a thiazide diuretic. A week later he has a coarse tremor, unsteadiness and confusion. What is the most likely cause?
o: Lithium toxicity from reduced lithium excretion
e: Correct. NSAIDs and thiazides raise lithium levels; lithium has a narrow therapeutic range.
Mania does not cause coarse tremor and ataxia.
Would not appear within a week after a drug change.
Requires serotonergic drugs.
Less likely with this drug history.
questions.obj: Lithium levels rise with NSAIDs, thiazides and dehydration; toxicity is a medical emergency (standard prescribing knowledge).

questions.stem: Which drug is a first-line option for bipolar I depression in the CANMAT/ISBD 2018 guidelines?
e: Correct. Lurasidone, lithium and lamotrigine are other first-line options.
Not a first-line option for bipolar depression.
Antidepressant monotherapy is not recommended in bipolar I disorder.
Not a bipolar depression treatment.
Not first-line.
questions.obj: Bipolar depression is treated differently from unipolar depression.

questions.stem: How do SSRIs such as sertraline work?
o: They block the serotonin transporter so serotonin stays longer in the synapse
e: Correct.
That is an MAO inhibitor.
That is esketamine or ketamine.
That is more like amphetamine-type drugs.
That is an antipsychotic.
questions.obj: SSRIs inhibit the serotonin transporter (SERT).

questions.stem: In a network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants for adults with major depression, what was found?
o: All were more effective than placebo, with modest differences between them
Only two were better than placebo
Effects were large and identical for all
e: Correct.
All 21 were better than placebo.
Incorrect.
Incorrect.
Effects were modest and varied somewhat.
questions.obj: Antidepressants work modestly better than placebo; choice is individual.

questions.stem: A woman in the EU has major depression that has not responded to two antidepressants. Her psychiatrist considers esketamine nasal spray. How is it used in the EU?
o: Together with an SSRI or SNRI
Always alone, never with other antidepressants
As a first treatment for mild depression
e: Correct. In the US it is also approved as monotherapy.
Not the EU indication.
It is for treatment-resistant depression.
It is a nasal spray given in a clinic.
Not its indication.
questions.obj: Esketamine (an NMDA antagonist) is used for treatment-resistant depression; regulatory details differ between the EU and US.

questions.stem: A man taking phenelzine (an MAO inhibitor) is started on fluoxetine. Within hours he has fever, agitation, tremor and muscle twitching. What is the diagnosis?
e: Correct. Combining an MAO inhibitor with an SSRI is dangerous.
Caused by antipsychotics; slower onset with rigidity.
He is not taking lithium.
Does not explain fever and muscle twitching.
Dry skin and urinary retention, not muscle twitching.
questions.obj: MAO inhibitors must not be combined with serotonergic drugs (standard prescribing knowledge).

questions.stem: Where is repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) usually applied for depression?
o: Over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
Over the primary motor cortex for mood
e: Correct.
Not a depression target.
Not a standard depression target.
That is an experimental deep brain stimulation target, not rTMS.
The motor cortex is used to set the stimulation dose, not as the treatment target.
questions.obj: rTMS for depression targets the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which connects to deeper mood circuits.

questions.stem: Which region (Brodmann area 25) is overactive in depression and has been an experimental deep brain stimulation target?
e: Correct.
Not involved in this way.
Not this target.
Not this target.
Auditory cortex.
questions.obj: The subgenual cingulate is a key node in mood regulation.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old autistic boy has severe tantrums, aggression and self-injury despite behavioural support. Which medicines have randomised-trial evidence for this irritability?
o: No medicine has ever been tested
e: Correct. Both reduced irritability; weight gain is common.
Not established for this indication.
Not shown to reduce irritability in autism trials.
Not relevant.
Several have been tested in trials.
questions.obj: Antipsychotics can reduce severe irritability in autism; they do not treat the core features.

questions.stem: Which statement about medicines and the core features of autism is correct?
o: No medicine treats the core features (social communication, restricted interests)
e: Correct. Care focuses on support, education and co-occurring conditions.
It reduces irritability only.
It treats hyperactivity.
It helps sleep.
No.
questions.obj: Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference; medicines target specific co-occurring problems.

questions.stem: An autistic 7-year-old takes 2 hours to fall asleep despite good sleep routines. Which treatment has trial evidence?
e: Correct. Children slept longer and fell asleep faster than with placebo.
Not a sleep treatment.
Can worsen sleep.
Not recommended for this.
Would worsen sleep.
questions.obj: Melatonin is used for insomnia in autism after behavioural steps.

questions.stem: How do ICD-11 and DSM-5 classify autism?
e: Correct. It begins in early development and persists through life.
Autism is not a psychosis.
It does not involve progressive loss of neurons.
No.
No.
questions.obj: Autism belongs to the neurodevelopmental disorders, alongside intellectual disability and ADHD.

Stimulates mood circuits magnetically (rTMS over the lateral prefrontal cortex) or electrically (ECT).
